core: Chattel slavery in the United States: enslaved people held as inheritable property for life, with enslaved status passed from mother to child
Scale of U.S. slavery: about 3.2 million enslaved people by 1850 and nearly 4 million (3,953,760) by 1860
Centrality of slavery to the U.S. economy: the cotton boom after the cotton gin (1793), 'King Cotton', and the expansion of plantation slavery across the Deep South
The domestic (internal) slave trade after the 1808 ban on importation, which forcibly moved roughly a million people from the Upper South to the Deep South and separated families
The humanity, agency, and resistance of enslaved people: family, faith, and culture; escape via the Underground Railroad; rebellions; and everyday resistance

How slavery drove the sectional crisis (Compromise of 1850, Fugitive Slave Act, Kansas-Nebraska Act, Dred Scott) toward the Civil War

Moral suasion and immediatism as abolitionist strategies; rejection of colonization

claims.claim: U.S. slavery was chattel slavery: enslaved people were treated as inheritable property held for life, and enslaved status was passed from an enslaved mother to her children, making bondage hereditary and permanent.
About 3.2 million people were enslaved in the United States by 1850, and the enslaved population grew to nearly four million (3,953,760) by the 1860 census.

Eli Whitney's cotton gin (patented 1793) made short-staple cotton profitable and fueled a cotton boom; by 1860 the South produced about two-thirds of the world's cotton, roughly 80 percent of the global supply, and about 75 percent of U.S. cotton was exported, making cotton central to the U.S. economy and prompting the boast that 'cotton is king.'

After Congress banned the importation of enslaved people from Africa effective January 1, 1808, a domestic (internal) slave trade forcibly moved roughly a million enslaved people from the Upper South to the Deep South; between 1790 and 1859 slaveholders in Virginia alone sold more than half a million people, routinely separating families.

Enslaved people asserted their humanity and resisted: they preserved family, faith (Christianity and spirituals invoking the Exodus), and culture (folktales, naming patterns, crafts); engaged in everyday resistance such as slowing work and breaking tools; and staged uprisings, including the 1811 German Coast (Deslondes) uprising in Louisiana and Nat Turner's rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia, in August 1831.

The Underground Railroad was resistance to enslavement through escape and flight; many freedom seekers began unaided, and after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 the network became more deliberate and organized. Harriet Tubman, who escaped slavery in 1849, returned to Maryland's Eastern Shore about 13 times between 1850 and 1860 and freed more than 70 family and friends.

Organized abolitionism grew in the 1830s: William Lloyd Garrison founded The Liberator in 1831 and the American Anti-Slavery Society was established in 1833 (about 250,000 members by 1838), championing immediate abolition and moral suasion while rejecting colonization. Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in 1838, published his Narrative in 1845, and founded the North Star in 1847; Sojourner Truth, born enslaved in New York about 1797 and free from 1827, became a noted abolitionist and women's-rights orator, delivering a famous speech at the 1851 Akron women's rights convention.

Conflict over slavery drove the sectional crisis toward the Civil War: the Compromise of 1850 (which included a harsh Fugitive Slave Act), the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and the Supreme Court's 1857 Dred Scott decision forced the question of slavery's expansion and enforcement onto the whole nation and deepened the divide between free and slave states.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact number and wording of Harriet Tubman's rescues are often exaggerated in popular accounts.
positions: Popular tradition (from Sarah Bradford's 1868 biography) claims Tubman freed about 300 people over 19 trips.
The National Park Service documents about 13 trips freeing more than 70 people, and treats the larger figures as estimates rather than sourced counts.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the NPS-documented figures (about 13 trips, more than 70 people) and does not repeat the inflated numbers.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The authenticity of the phrase 'Ain't I a Woman?' attributed to Sojourner Truth's 1851 Akron speech.
positions: The widely quoted version, including the refrain 'Ain't I a Woman?', was published by Frances Gage in 1863, twelve years after the speech.
Marius Robinson's account, published about a month after the speech in the Anti-Slavery Bugle, does not contain that phrase.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson notes that Truth gave a famous 1851 speech but flags that the celebrated wording comes from an 1863 retelling and is disputed, rather than quoting it as verbatim.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. History, 12.2 African Americans in the Antebellum United States
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-20. Supports: slavery described as a dehumanizing crime against humanity; enslaved people faced sale, whipping, and psychological terror; constant fear of family separation; everyday resistance (breaking tools, feigning ignorance); the 1811 Louisiana (German Coast) uprising led by Charles Deslondes with as many as five hundred participants; Nat Turner's rebellion beginning August 22, 1831, in Southampton County, Virginia; cultural survival through Brer Rabbit folktales, Christianity and Exodus-themed songs, and African naming patterns and basketry; about 3.2 million enslaved by 1850. REFERENCE_ONLY; original synthesis, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is the Underground Railroad?
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. federal agency page (public domain). Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-20. Supports: the Underground Railroad as resistance to enslavement through escape and flight; many freedom seekers began unaided and self-emancipated; the network became more deliberate and organized after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850; help came from people of all races, classes, and genders; freedom seekers went to Canada, Mexico, Spanish Florida, and elsewhere. No prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Harriet Tubman - Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad National Historical Park
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. federal agency page (public domain). Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-20. Supports: Araminta Ross (Harriet Tubman) born enslaved in 1822 in Dorchester County, Maryland; escaped alone in the fall of 1849 to Philadelphia; between 1850 and 1860 returned to Maryland's Eastern Shore 13 times and freed more than 70 family and friends; later freed over 750 people in an 1863 Civil War raid. No prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Frederick Douglass National Historic Site - Biography
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. federal agency page (public domain). Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-20. Supports: Douglass born into slavery on Maryland's Eastern Shore (February 1817, named Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey); escaped bondage in 1838 at age 21 and adopted a new surname; agent for the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society from 1841; published the Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass in 1845; became editor and publisher of the North Star in Rochester, New York, after 1847. No prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Sojourner Truth: Ain't I A Woman?
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. federal agency page (public domain). Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-20. Supports: born Isabella Baumfree about 1797 on a New York estate; departed slavery in 1827 after her enslaver broke promises tied to the New York gradual-abolition law; took the name Sojourner Truth in 1843 after a religious conversion; abolition and women's-rights advocacy by the 1850s; delivered a famous speech at the 1851 Women's Rights Convention in Akron, Ohio. The page notes the 'Ain't I a Woman?' wording comes from Frances Gage's 1863 version, twelve years later, and that Marius Robinson's 1851 account (Anti-Slavery Bugle) lacks the phrase. No prose reproduced.
